query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing 2 at.% of Mo with Re in a W–Ta–Mo–Nb–V refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) intermediate layer will raise its through-thickness thermal conductivity by ≥25 % at 800 °C while retaining ≥90 % of its 0.2 % yield strength, compared with the undoped alloy processed identically.
generation.material_initial_state: Vacuum-arc-melted, homogenised (1400 °C, 24 h) equiatomic W–Ta–Mo–Nb–V RHEA plate, 10 mm thick, unirradiated, as-cast microstructure with ~50 µm grains.
generation.intervention: Micro-alloying: substitute 2 at.% Re for Mo (final nominal composition W20Ta20Mo18Re2Nb20V20, homogenised under the same schedule).
generation.conditions: Steady heat flux in high-vacuum; bulk temperatures 600–1000 °C; macroscopic tensile stress ≤50 MPa; no neutron or ion irradiation during the measurement window.
generation.structural_mediator: Slightly reduced lattice distortion and anti-site defect concentration in the single-phase BCC solid solution due to atomic-size and electronic matching of Re with W, yielding longer electron mean free paths.
generation.mechanism: Re atoms (i) decrease local strain fields that scatter conduction electrons, and (ii) raise the valence-electron concentration, increasing the electronic contribution to κ. Because Re is solution-strengthening and chemically compatible, the solid-solution hardening of the BCC matrix is preserved, so tensile strength is not sacrificed.
generation.predicted_outcome: At 800 °C the laser-flash-derived thermal conductivity of the Re-doped alloy will be ≥44 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ versus ~35 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ for the baseline, while the 0.2 % yield strength remains ≥450 MPa (≥90 % of the baseline ~500 MPa). Similar ≥20 % κ gains persist from 600 to 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: Same alloy without Re addition, identically melted, homogenised and tested.
generation.boundary: Effect expected up to ~1000 °C and ≤0.1 dpa irradiation. Above 1100 °C or under prolonged neutron exposure, Re segregation or σ-phase precipitation may negate the benefit.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of κ improvement may be lower if disorder scattering dominates; Re might cluster under service irradiation, erasing the conductivity gain.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two 30 mm × 30 mm × 3 mm coupons: (a) baseline W–Ta–Mo–Nb–V and (b) Re-doped variant. Homogenise identically. Measure density (Archimedes), specific heat (DSC), and thermal diffusivity (laser flash) at 600, 800, and 1000 °C to calculate κ=αρCp. Perform tensile tests at 800 °C (strain-rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹) on sub-size ASTM E8 specimens cut from each coupon.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if (i) κ_Re / κ_baseline < 1.10 at all measured temperatures OR (ii) σ0.2_Re < 0.9 × σ0.2_baseline.
